claim: Vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) and Sindbis virus (SINV) are completely restricted in their replication after entry into Lepidopteran cells.
source: We found that two RNA viruses with broad host ranges, vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) and Sindbis virus (SINV), are completely restricted in their replication after entry into Lepidopteran cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing low levels of GFP-positive cells and viral gene expression in single infections, as well as detection of viral capsids inside cells by confocal microscopy.

claim: The restriction of VSV and SINV replication in Lepidopteran cells is overcome when cells are co-infected with vaccinia virus (VACV).
source: This restriction is overcome when cells are co-infected with vaccinia virus (VACV), a vertebrate DNA virus.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing increased GFP-positive cells, LUC activity, viral protein levels, and virus titers during VACV co-infection.

claim: Lepidopteran RNAi pathways restrict RNA virus infection.
source: Using RNAi screening, we show that Lepidopteran RNAi, Nuclear Factor-κB, and ubiquitin-proteasome pathways restrict RNA virus infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNAi knockdown experiments showing that silencing of AGO2 and Dicer-2 increased viral gene expression.

claim: Lepidopteran Nuclear Factor-κB pathways restrict RNA virus infection.
source: Using RNAi screening, we show that Lepidopteran RNAi, Nuclear Factor-κB, and ubiquitin-proteasome pathways restrict RNA virus infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNAi knockdown experiments showing that silencing of Relish (NF-κB homolog) increased viral gene expression.

claim: Lepidopteran ubiquitin-proteasome pathways restrict RNA virus infection.
source: Using RNAi screening, we show that Lepidopteran RNAi, Nuclear Factor-κB, and ubiquitin-proteasome pathways restrict RNA virus infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNAi knockdown experiments showing that silencing of Effete and ubiquitin-encoding genes increased viral gene expression, as well as experiments with proteasome inhibitors.

claim: VACV protein A51R can partially overcome the restriction of RNA virus replication in Lepidopteran cells.
source: Surprisingly, a highly conserved, uncharacterized VACV protein, A51R, can partially overcome this virus restriction.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNAi screening and genetic deletion studies showing that A51R is necessary and sufficient for RNA virus rescue.

claim: A51R is critical for VACV replication in vertebrate cells.
source: We show that A51R is also critical for VACV replication in vertebrate cells and for pathogenesis in mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from growth curve analyses showing reduced replication of ΔA51R strain in BSC-40 cells.

claim: A51R is critical for VACV pathogenesis in mice.
source: We show that A51R is also critical for VACV replication in vertebrate cells and for pathogenesis in mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mouse infection studies showing reduced mortality and viral loads in tissues of mice infected with ΔA51R strain.

claim: A51R colocalizes with host microtubules.
source: Interestingly, A51R colocalizes with, and stabilizes, host microtubules and also associates with ubiquitin.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from confocal microscopy showing overlap of A51R staining with tubulin staining.

claim: A51R stabilizes host microtubules.
source: Interestingly, A51R colocalizes with, and stabilizes, host microtubules and also associates with ubiquitin.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that A51R-expressing cells contain nocodazole-resistant and vincristine-resistant microtubule structures.

claim: A51R associates with ubiquitin.
source: Interestingly, A51R colocalizes with, and stabilizes, host microtubules and also associates with ubiquitin.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mass spectrometry analysis of A51R immunoprecipitates showing ubiquitin as one of the most enriched proteins.

claim: Less than 4% of LD652 cells exhibited GFP fluorescence by 96 hours post-infection with VSV-GFP or SINV-GFP at MOI of 10.
source: In single infections with VSV-GFP (Kato et al., 2005) or SINV-GFP (Cristea et al., 2006), we found that, even at a high multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 10, <4% of LD652 cells exhibited GFP fluorescence by 96 hr post-infection (hpi) (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,B and cited references for the virus strains used.

claim: Co-infection with VACV-WR increased GFP-positive cells to approximately 77% for VSV-GFP and approximately 45% for SINV-GFP by 96 hpi.
source: Consistent with this idea, when LD652 cells were co-infected with VSV-GFP or SINV-GFP and the Western Reserve (WR) strain of VACV (VACV-WR), the number of GFP-positive cells increased to ∼77% (VSV-GFP) and ∼45% (SINV-GFP) by 96 hpi (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: VACV enters LD652 cells and reaches the stage of late gene expression but ultimately fails to complete virion morphogenesis.
source: A previous report indicated that VACV enters LD652 cells and reaches the stage of late gene expression but ultimately fails to complete virion morphogenesis (Li et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Poxviruses encode numerous immunomodulatory proteins that inhibit a wide variety of host antiviral pathways.
source: VACV, like other poxviruses, encodes numerous immunomodulatory proteins that inhibit a wide variety of host antiviral pathways (Smith et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established scientific knowledge.

claim: VSV and SINV capsids were detected inside singly-infected LD652 cells using confocal microscopy.
source: Consistent with this, we detected VSV and SINV capsids inside singly-infected LD652 cells using confocal microscopy (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: At 8 hpi, RT-PCR analysis detected similar levels of VSV and SINV viral transcripts with or without VACV-WR co-infection.
source: Furthermore, at 8 hpi RT-PCR analysis of VSV- and SINV-infected cells detected a similar level of viral transcripts with or without VACV-WR co-infection (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: VSV and SINV gene expression can be rescued by addition of VACV-WR as late as 24 hpi with RNA virus.
source: Remarkably, we could also rescue VSV and SINV gene expression (albeit to reduced levels) by the addition of VACV-WR as late as 24 hpi with RNA virus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: RNA virus restriction in LD652 cells occurs post-entry.
source: Together these data indicate that RNA virus restriction occurs post-entry.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from multiple experimental observations including detection of viral capsids inside cells and viral transcripts at early time points.

claim: Actinomycin D at 0.1 μg/ml reduced LD652 cell viability by approximately 50% after 48 hours of treatment.
source: We chose an ActD dose range such that the highest dose (0.1 μg/ml) reduced cell viability by ∼50% after 48 hr of treatment (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Higher doses of actinomycin D enhanced viral gene expression by as much as approximately 100-fold compared to control treatments.
source: We found that the higher ActD doses enhanced viral gene expression by as much as ∼100-fold compared to control treatments (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Host cell transcription is required for LD652 resistance to RNA virus infection.
source: These results suggest that host cell transcription is required for LD652 resistance to RNA virus infection and that LD652 cells express antiviral immunity factors.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that blocking transcription with actinomycin D enhanced viral replication.

claim: LD652 cells express antiviral immunity factors.
source: These results suggest that host cell transcription is required for LD652 resistance to RNA virus infection and that LD652 cells express antiviral immunity factors.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that blocking transcription with actinomycin D enhanced viral replication.

claim: Actinomycin D treatment can induce apoptosis in invertebrate cells.
source: It should be noted that ActD treatment can induce apoptosis in invertebrate cells (Wang et al., 2008) and previous studies have found apoptosis induction to enhance SINV replication in mosquitoes (Wang et al., 2012), thus it is possible that the enhanced viral replication observed in the presence of ActD may be in part due to apoptosis induction in LD652 cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Apoptosis induction has been found to enhance SINV replication in mosquitoes.
source: It should be noted that ActD treatment can induce apoptosis in invertebrate cells (Wang et al., 2008) and previous studies have found apoptosis induction to enhance SINV replication in mosquitoes (Wang et al., 2012), thus it is possible that the enhanced viral replication observed in the presence of ActD may be in part due to apoptosis induction in LD652 cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The enhanced viral replication observed in the presence of actinomycin D may be in part due to apoptosis induction in LD652 cells.
source: It should be noted that ActD treatment can induce apoptosis in invertebrate cells (Wang et al., 2008) and previous studies have found apoptosis induction to enhance SINV replication in mosquitoes (Wang et al., 2012), thus it is possible that the enhanced viral replication observed in the presence of ActD may be in part due to apoptosis induction in LD652 cells.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from cited studies.

claim: RNAi knockdown of AGO2 increased LUC expression approximately 10-fold in both VSV-LUC- and SINV-LUC-infected cells.
source: Knockdowns of four transcripts, encoding homologs of the RNAi pathway proteins AGO2 and Dicer-2 (Kingsolver et al., 2013), the Nuclear Factor kappa B (NF-κB)-homolog Relish (Dushay et al., 1996), and the E2 ubiquitin (Ub)-conjugating enzyme Effete (Treier et al., 1992), increased LUC expression ∼10-fold in both VSV-LUC- and SINV-LUC-infected cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNAi knockdown experiments and citations for the protein identities.

claim: RNAi knockdown of Dicer-2 increased LUC expression approximately 10-fold in both VSV-LUC- and SINV-LUC-infected cells.
source: Knockdowns of four transcripts, encoding homologs of the RNAi pathway proteins AGO2 and Dicer-2 (Kingsolver et al., 2013), the Nuclear Factor kappa B (NF-κB)-homolog Relish (Dushay et al., 1996), and the E2 ubiquitin (Ub)-conjugating enzyme Effete (Treier et al., 1992), increased LUC expression ∼10-fold in both VSV-LUC- and SINV-LUC-infected cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNAi knockdown experiments and citations for the protein identities.

claim: RNAi knockdown of Relish increased LUC expression approximately 10-fold in both VSV-LUC- and SINV-LUC-infected cells.
source: Knockdowns of four transcripts, encoding homologs of the RNAi pathway proteins AGO2 and Dicer-2 (Kingsolver et al., 2013), the Nuclear Factor kappa B (NF-κB)-homolog Relish (Dushay et al., 1996), and the E2 ubiquitin (Ub)-conjugating enzyme Effete (Treier et al., 1992), increased LUC expression ∼10-fold in both VSV-LUC- and SINV-LUC-infected cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNAi knockdown experiments and citations for the protein identities.

claim: RNAi knockdown of Effete increased LUC expression approximately 10-fold in both VSV-LUC- and SINV-LUC-infected cells.
source: Knockdowns of four transcripts, encoding homologs of the RNAi pathway proteins AGO2 and Dicer-2 (Kingsolver et al., 2013), the Nuclear Factor kappa B (NF-κB)-homolog Relish (Dushay et al., 1996), and the E2 ubiquitin (Ub)-conjugating enzyme Effete (Treier et al., 1992), increased LUC expression ∼10-fold in both VSV-LUC- and SINV-LUC-infected cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNAi knockdown experiments and citations for the protein identities.

claim: RNAi-targeting Polyubiquitin, Ub-RPL40 and Ub-RPS27A increased LUC expression nearly 1000-fold in VSV-LUC-infected cells.
source: RNAi-targeting three Ub-encoding genes, including Polyubiquitin, Ub-RPL40 and Ub-RPS27A increased LUC expression nearly 1000-fold in VSV-LUC-infected cells (Figure 2C) and 10-fold in SINV-LUC-infected cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: RNAi-targeting Polyubiquitin, Ub-RPL40 and Ub-RPS27A increased LUC expression 10-fold in SINV-LUC-infected cells.
source: RNAi-targeting three Ub-encoding genes, including Polyubiquitin, Ub-RPL40 and Ub-RPS27A increased LUC expression nearly 1000-fold in VSV-LUC-infected cells (Figure 2C) and 10-fold in SINV-LUC-infected cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Ub-RPL40 and Ub-RPS27A encode highly conserved fusion proteins that are cleaved by endogenous proteases into free ubiquitin and ribosomal proteins.
source: Ub-RPL40 and Ub-RPS27A encode highly conserved fusion proteins that are cleaved by endogenous proteases into free Ub and either ribosomal protein L40 (RPL40) or ribosomal protein S27A (RPS27A), components of the 60S and 40S ribosomal subunits, respectively (Finley et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established scientific knowledge.

claim: The dramatic effect of ubiquitin RNAi on LUC expression in VSV-LUC-infected cells was not caused by increased LUC protein stability due to inhibition of the ubiquitin-proteasome system.
source: The dramatic effect of Ub RNAi on LUC expression in VSV-LUC-infected cells was not caused by increased LUC protein stability due to inhibition of the Ub-proteasome system (UPS) (See Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Viral-driven, but not plasmid-driven LUC expression was enhanced in experiments aimed at inhibiting the UPS.
source: We found that viral-driven, but not plasmid-driven (p166-LUC), LUC expression was enhanced in experiments aimed at inhibiting the UPS, including: (i) exposure to Ub RNAi (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), (ii) treatment with inhibitors of either E1 Ub-activating enzymes (PYR-41; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) (Yang et al., 2007), or the proteasome (MG132; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) (Lee and Goldberg, 1998), and finally, by (iii) transient expression of a wild-type (but not a catalytically inactive) coronavirus-encoded deubiquitinase (PLpro; Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) (Barretto et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and citations for the inhibitors and deubiquitinase used.

claim: Host restriction of RNA virus replication in LD652 cells is mediated by multiple host factors including those involved in RNAi-, NF-κB, and ubiquitin-related pathways.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that host restriction of RNA virus replication in LD652 cells is mediated by multiple host factors including those involved in RNAi-, NF-κB, and Ub-related pathways.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the RNAi knockdown experiments and UPS inhibition experiments.

claim: Heat-inactivated VACV failed to rescue VSV and SINV replication.
source: Heat inactivated VACV, which can enter cells but cannot express its genes (Dales and Kajioka, 1964), failed to rescue VSV and SINV replication (Figure 3A), indicating that VACV gene expression was required for rescue.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and citation for the heat inactivation method.

claim: VACV gene expression is required for rescue of VSV and SINV replication in LD652 cells.
source: Heat inactivated VACV, which can enter cells but cannot express its genes (Dales and Kajioka, 1964), failed to rescue VSV and SINV replication (Figure 3A), indicating that VACV gene expression was required for rescue.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that heat-inactivated VACV failed to rescue RNA virus replication.

claim: Inhibiting post-replicative VACV gene expression with AraC did not prevent rescue of either VSV or SINV.
source: We found that inhibiting post-replicative VACV gene expression did not prevent rescue of either VSV or SINV (Figure 3B), narrowing the RNA virus rescue activity to one or more of the 118 early VACV genes (Yang et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and citation for the number of early VACV genes.

claim: The RNA virus rescue activity is narrowed to one or more of the 118 early VACV genes.
source: We found that inhibiting post-replicative VACV gene expression did not prevent rescue of either VSV or SINV (Figure 3B), narrowing the RNA virus rescue activity to one or more of the 118 early VACV genes (Yang et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the AraC experiment and citation for the number of early VACV genes.

claim: VACV-MVA failed to fully rescue either VSV or SINV compared to VACV-WR or Copenhagen strains.
source: We found that the attenuated modified VACV strain Ankara (VACV-MVA) (Antoine et al., 1998) failed to fully rescue either VSV or SINV as compared to either VACV-WR or Copenhagen strains (Figure 3C,D), despite similar levels of viral gene expression by all three VACV strains (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C,D,E and citation for VACV-MVA.

claim: VACV-MVA is defective for one or more factors required for RNA virus rescue in LD652 cells.
source: These results suggested that VACV-MVA is defective for one or more factors required for RNA virus rescue in LD652 cells.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that VACV-MVA failed to fully rescue RNA viruses despite similar gene expression levels.

claim: RNAi of A51R caused RNA virus gene expression to drop by approximately 95% for VSV and by approximately 69% for SINV.
source: RNAi of a single, uncharacterized VACV gene, A51R, caused RNA virus gene expression to drop below an arbitrary cut off of 50% of the control (GFP) RNAi treatment. The A51R knockdown reduced virus gene expression by ∼95% (VSV) and by ∼69% (SINV) (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Co-infection with ΔA51R resulted in a 100-fold reduction in VSV gene expression relative to co-infection with VACV-WR.
source: Importantly, we found that co-infection with ΔA51R resulted in a 100-fold reduction in VSV gene expression relative to co-infection with VACV-WR (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: VSV was rescued by co-infecting with revertant VACV strains expressing Flag-tagged A51R.
source: VSV was rescued by co-infecting with revertant VACV strains (Figure 4C), expressing a Flag-tagged A51R gene (Flag-A51R) reintroduced into either the A51R locus (ΔA51RFA51R) or the VACV thymidine kinase (J2R) locus (ΔJ2R/ΔA51RFA51R).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Flag-A51R and Flag-MVAA51R proteins migrated as single bands of approximately 38 and 35 kDa, respectively, on immunoblots.
source: Flag-A51R and Flag-MVAA51R proteins migrated as single bands of ∼38 and 35 kDa, respectively, on immunoblots (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B,C.

claim: The lower molecular weight of the VACV-MVA A51R protein is likely due to a C-terminal truncation of approximately 20 amino acids.
source: The lower molecular weight of the VACV-MVA protein is likely due to a C-terminal truncation of ∼20 amino acids that results from a genomic deletion that occurred during VACV-MVA passage in culture (Antoine et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observed molecular weight difference and citation to a study describing VACV-MVA genomic deletions.

claim: The ΔJ2R/ΔA51RFMVAA51R strain failed to fully rescue VSV.
source: Furthermore, consistent with the idea that the VACV-MVA A51R protein is not functional, we found that the ΔJ2R/ΔA51RFMVAA51R strain failed to fully rescue VSV (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Flag-A51R is expressed early in VACV infection.
source: Importantly, immunoblot of lysates from a time course of A51RFA51R infection confirmed that Flag-A51R is expressed early in VACV infection, as it was detected by 2 hpi in the absence or presence of AraC (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D.

claim: A51R is an early VACV protein necessary to relieve the restriction of VSV in LD652 cells.
source: Together these results indicate that A51R is an early VACV protein necessary to relieve the restriction of VSV in LD652 cells.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from multiple experimental observations including RNAi, deletion, and reversion studies.

claim: A51R is required for full rescue of SINV replication by VACV.
source: A51R was also required for full rescue of SINV replication by VACV (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: ΔA51R and ΔJ2R/ΔA51RFMVAA51R strains exhibited only a moderate fourfold reduction in their ability to promote SINV gene expression compared to 100-fold reductions for VSV.
source: However, we noticed that ΔA51R and ΔJ2R/ΔA51RFMVAA51R strains exhibited only a moderate fourfold reduction in their ability to promote SINV gene expression as compared to 100-fold reductions for VSV (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Other VACV factors in addition to A51R promote SINV replication in LD652 cells.
source: These findings suggest that other VACV factors in addition to A51R promote SINV replication in LD652 cells.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that A51R deletion had a smaller effect on SINV than on VSV rescue.

claim: Expression of Flag-A51R resulted in an approximately 60-fold increase in VSV gene expression relative to control transfections.
source: Although only ∼40–60% of cells expressed detectable Flag-A51R protein (data not shown), we observed an ∼60-fold increase in VSV and 12-fold increase in SINV gene expression relative to control transfections with empty p166 vector or vector encoding Flag-tagged GFP (Flag-GFP) (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Expression of Flag-A51R resulted in a 12-fold increase in SINV gene expression relative to control transfections.
source: Although only ∼40–60% of cells expressed detectable Flag-A51R protein (data not shown), we observed an ∼60-fold increase in VSV and 12-fold increase in SINV gene expression relative to control transfections with empty p166 vector or vector encoding Flag-tagged GFP (Flag-GFP) (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Flag-A51R expression is sufficient to overcome the host restriction to RNA virus replication in the absence of other VACV proteins.
source: These results indicate that Flag-A51R expression is sufficient to overcome the host restriction to RNA virus replication in the absence of other VACV proteins.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that transfection of Flag-A51R alone enhanced RNA virus replication.

claim: Transfection of Flag-GFP or Flag-A51R constructs into LD652 cells did not lead to notable changes in cell viability over a 7 day time course.
source: Transfection of Flag-GFP or Flag-A51R constructs into LD652 cells did not lead to notable changes in cell viability over a 7 day time course.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cell viability assays.

claim: When Flag-A51R-transfected cells were infected with VSV-LUC, cell viability began to drop by 96 hpi, ultimately reaching cell viabilities of approximately 50% by day 7 of infection.
source: However, when transfected cells were subsequently infected with VSV-LUC, cell viability began to drop by 96 hpi, ultimately reaching cell viabilities of ∼50% by day 7 of infection (Figure 4I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Reduced cell viability was not observed when Flag-GFP-transfected cells were infected with VSV-LUC.
source: This reduced cell viability was not observed when Flag-GFP-transfected cells were infected with VSV-LUC, suggesting that active viral replication was required to induce cell death (Figure 4I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Active viral replication is required to induce cell death in Flag-A51R-transfected LD652 cells.
source: This reduced cell viability was not observed when Flag-GFP-transfected cells were infected with VSV-LUC, suggesting that active viral replication was required to induce cell death (Figure 4I).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that cell death only occurred when A51R-expressing cells were infected with virus.

claim: A51R genes are found in most vertebrate poxvirus genera.
source: A51R genes are found in most vertebrate poxvirus genera (Table 1) yet absent in the genomes of entomopoxviruses (not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: A51R genes are absent in the genomes of entomopoxviruses.
source: A51R genes are found in most vertebrate poxvirus genera (Table 1) yet absent in the genomes of entomopoxviruses (not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis of entomopoxvirus genomes.

claim: A51R homologs from different poxviruses with amino acid identities ranging from 90% to 30% relative to VACV-WR A51R enhanced VSV gene expression to a similar level.
source: Strikingly, we found that A51R from each poxvirus enhanced VSV gene expression to a similar level (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The ability of A51R to overcome the LD652 restriction to VSV infection is a conserved function of distantly-related A51R homologs.
source: Thus, the ability of A51R to overcome the LD652 restriction to VSV infection is a conserved function of distantly-related A51R homologs.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that A51R homologs from different poxviruses all enhanced VSV replication.

claim: A51R expression relieved restriction to VSV replication in L. dispar embryonic cell line (LdEP).
source: Indeed, we found that A51R expression relieved restriction to VSV replication in each of the three additional Lepidopteran cell lines tested, including an L. dispar embryonic cell line (LdEP) (Figure 6A), a Spodoptera frugiperda-derived cell line (Sf9) (Figure 6B,C), and a Manduca sexta-derived cell line (GV-1) (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: A51R expression relieved restriction to VSV replication in Spodoptera frugiperda-derived cell line (Sf9).
source: Indeed, we found that A51R expression relieved restriction to VSV replication in each of the three additional Lepidopteran cell lines tested, including an L. dispar embryonic cell line (LdEP) (Figure 6A), a Spodoptera frugiperda-derived cell line (Sf9) (Figure 6B,C), and a Manduca sexta-derived cell line (GV-1) (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: A51R expression relieved restriction to VSV replication in Manduca sexta-derived cell line (GV-1).
source: Indeed, we found that A51R expression relieved restriction to VSV replication in each of the three additional Lepidopteran cell lines tested, including an L. dispar embryonic cell line (LdEP) (Figure 6A), a Spodoptera frugiperda-derived cell line (Sf9) (Figure 6B,C), and a Manduca sexta-derived cell line (GV-1) (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D,E.

claim: A51R expression did not enhance VSV replication in D. melanogaster-derived DL1 cells.
source: In contrast, A51R expression did not enhance VSV replication in D. melanogaster-derived DL1 cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), despite significant expression of Flag-A51R protein (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: VSV gene expression in DL1 cells was not enhanced by co-infection with VACV-WR.
source: VSV gene expression in DL1 cells was also not enhanced by co-infection with VACV-WR (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Flag-A51R formed both aggregate-like as well as filamentous structures in the cytoplasm of BSC-40 cells.
source: We found that Flag-A51R, expressed under its natural promoter from the ΔA51RFA51R virus, formed both aggregate-like as well as filamentous structures in the cytoplasm of African green monkey-derived (BSC-40) cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from confocal microscopy.

claim: Flag-A51R staining pattern significantly overlapped with that of cellular tubulin.
source: This staining pattern significantly overlapped with that of cellular tubulin, suggesting that A51R associates with a subset of MTs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A51R associates with a subset of microtubules.
source: This staining pattern significantly overlapped with that of cellular tubulin, suggesting that A51R associates with a subset of MTs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation of overlapping staining patterns.

claim: Deconvolution of images revealed Flag-A51R staining localized on intact microtubule tracks.
source: Indeed deconvolution of images from these experiments revealed Flag-A51R staining localized on intact MT tracks (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In the presence of nocodazole, microtubule structures were essentially absent in mock-infected and ΔA51R-infected cells.
source: In the presence of nocodazole, MT structures were essentially absent in mock-infected and ΔA51R-infected cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from microscopy of nocodazole-treated cells.

claim: Filamentous, drug-resistant microtubule pieces were abundant in ΔA51RFA51R-infected BSC-40 cells treated with nocodazole.
source: However filamentous, drug-resistant 'MT pieces' were abundant in ΔA51RFA51R-infected BSC-40 cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Nocodazole-resistant microtubule pieces were previously observed in mammalian cells infected with VACV-WR but not with VACV-MVA.
source: Nocodazole-resistant MT pieces were previously observed in mammalian cells infected with VACV-WR but not with VACV-MVA (Ploubidou et al., 2000; Schepis et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Flag-MVAA51R stained small punctate structures throughout the cytoplasm that overlapped with tubulin in nocodazole-treated cells.
source: We therefore examined Flag-MVAA51R protein localization in nocodazole-treated cells and found that, although Flag-MVAA51R staining stained small punctate structures throughout the cytoplasm that overlapped with tubulin, large drug-resistant MT-like structures failed to form (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Large drug-resistant microtubule-like structures failed to form in cells expressing Flag-MVAA51R.
source: We therefore examined Flag-MVAA51R protein localization in nocodazole-treated cells and found that, although Flag-MVAA51R staining stained small punctate structures throughout the cytoplasm that overlapped with tubulin, large drug-resistant MT-like structures failed to form (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Flag-MVAA51R protein is deficient in its ability to both form filament-like structures and to protect microtubules from depolymerization.
source: These results suggest that Flag-MVAA51R protein is deficient in its ability to both form filament-like structures and to protect MTs from depolymerization.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that Flag-MVAA51R failed to form drug-resistant MT structures.

claim: Flag-A51R expression is sufficient for both localization to and stabilization of microtubules.
source: We found that Flag-A51R expression was sufficient for both localization to, and stabilization of, MTs (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A from transfection experiments.

claim: A51R homologs from other poxviruses also co-localize with and protect microtubules from depolymerization.
source: Moreover, using similar assays, we found that A51R homologs from other poxviruses also co-localize with and protect MTs from depolymerization (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B.

claim: In LD652 cells, Flag-A51R formed aggregates and filamentous structures that co-localized with and protected microtubules from depolymerization by vincristine.
source: Finally, in LD652 cells, as in vertebrate cells, Flag-A51R formed aggregates and filamentous structures that co-localized with and protected MTs from depolymerization by the MT-depolymerizing agent vincristine (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The ability of A51R to interact with the host microtubule cytoskeleton is a conserved property of A51R proteins.
source: Taken together, our findings suggest that the ability of A51R to interact with the host MT cytoskeleton is a conserved property of A51R proteins.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from observations in multiple cell types and with multiple A51R homologs.

claim: Alanine substitution of residue R321 produced a Flag-A51RR321A mutant with reduced VSV rescue phenotype compared to Flag-A51R.
source: However, alanine substitution of residue R321, which lies within the C-terminal region of A51R that is missing in VACV-MVA A51R (Figure 8A), produced a suitable mutant for analysis. Flag-A51RR321A proteins displayed a reduced VSV rescue phenotype when compared to Flag-A51R proteins (Figure 8B) despite similar levels of expression (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A,B,C.

claim: Both Flag-A51R and Flag-A51RR321A formed filamentous structures that overlapped with tubulin staining in the presence of vincristine.
source: Importantly, when expressed in LD652 cells in the presence of vincristine, both Flag-A51R (Figure 8D; Video 1) and Flag-A51RR321A (Figure 8D; Video 2) formed filamentous structures that overlapped with tubulin staining (Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: Microtubule stabilization alone is insufficient to promote full RNA virus rescue.
source: These results suggest that MT stabilization alone is insufficient to promote full RNA virus rescue.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that A51RR321A mutant stabilizes MTs but has reduced rescue activity.

claim: The four most-enriched proteins in Flag-A51R immunoprecipitates are Flag-A51R, myosin II essential light chain, ubiquitin, and ribosomal protein S15.
source: Filtering differential normalized spectral abundance factor (NSAF) (Zybailov et al., 2006) values from both control and Flag-A51R immunoprecipitates identified the four most-enriched proteins in Flag-A51R treatments. These proteins are the target Flag-A51R, myosin II essential light chain (a constituent of the actomyosin cytoskeleton [Clark et al., 2007]), Ub, and ribosomal protein S15 (a component of the 40S subunit of the ribosome that has also been shown to modulate the activity of specific E3 ubiquitin ligases [Daftuar et al., 2013]) (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mass spectrometry shown in Table 2 and citations for protein identities.

claim: Radiolabeled VSV N protein was undetectable in cells infected only with either VACV-WR or VSV-LUC.
source: We found that radiolabeled VSV N protein was undetectable in cells infected only with either VACV-WR (control) or VSV-LUC.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from radiolabeling experiments.

claim: Significant quantities of radiolabeled VSV N protein were found in VSV-LUC-infected cells that were also infected with either VACV-WR or ΔA51R strains.
source: In contrast, we found significant quantities of radiolabeled VSV N protein in VSV-LUC-infected cells that were also infected with either VACV-WR or ΔA51R strains (Figure 9A, top panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Viral protein translation rates are too low to be detected by radiolabeling in VSV-LUC single infections but are detectable in co-infections with VACV-WR or ΔA51R strains.
source: These results suggest that viral protein translation rates are too low to be detected by this method in VSV-LUC single infections but are detectable (and surprisingly similar) in co-infections with VACV-WR or ΔA51R strains.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the radiolabeling experiments.

claim: Total VSV N protein levels were dramatically reduced in ΔA51R co-infections compared to co-infections with VACV-WR.
source: However, total VSV N protein levels were dramatically reduced in ΔA51R co-infections compared to co-infections with VACV-WR (Figure 9A, middle panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: The half-life of VSV N protein is approximately 5.3 hours during co-infection with VACV-WR.
source: Regression analyses of pulse-chase experiments estimated the half-life of VSV N to be ∼5.3 hr during co-infection with VACV-WR while only ∼1.8 hr during co-infection with the ΔA51R strain.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from pulse-chase experiments and regression analysis.

claim: The half-life of VSV N protein is approximately 1.8 hours during co-infection with the ΔA51R strain.
source: Regression analyses of pulse-chase experiments estimated the half-life of VSV N to be ∼5.3 hr during co-infection with VACV-WR while only ∼1.8 hr during co-infection with the ΔA51R strain.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from pulse-chase experiments and regression analysis.

claim: A51R associates with ubiquitin and promotes viral protein stability.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that A51R associates with Ub and promotes viral protein stability.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from mass spectrometry and pulse-chase experiments.

claim: At a low MOI of 0.03, ΔA51R titers began to plateau at 24 hpi while VACV-WR and ΔA51RFA51R titers continued to increase to approximately 100-fold higher levels by 72 hpi.
source: At a low MOI of 0.03, the ΔA51R, VACV-WR, and ΔA51RFA51R strains replicated with similar kinetics until 24 hpi at which point ΔA51R titers began to plateau. In contrast, VACV-WR and ΔA51RFA51R titers continued to increase to ∼100-fold higher levels by 72 hpi (Figure 10A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10A.

claim: At a higher MOI of 3, the plateau of ΔA51R titer occurred earlier, at 12 hpi.
source: This plateau of ΔA51R titer was also observed at a higher MOI of 3, but occurred earlier, at 12 hpi (Figure 10B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10B.

claim: A51R promotes VACV replication in vertebrate cell culture.
source: These results indicate that A51R promotes VACV replication in vertebrate cell culture.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the growth curve analyses.

claim: In animals infected with VACV-WR, weight loss continued on days 6-7 post-infection, with 5/5 animals ultimately succumbing to infection by day 7.
source: In animals infected with VACV-WR, weight loss continued on days 6–7 post-infection, with 5/5 animals ultimately succumbing to infection by day 7.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mouse infection studies.

claim: Only 1/5 animals infected with the ΔA51R strain died by day 7, while the remaining animals recovered from infection, gained weight and survived until the end of the 28 day experiment.
source: In contrast, only 1/5 animals infected with the ΔA51R strain died by day 7, while the remaining animals recovered from infection, gained weight (Figure 10C) and survived until the end of the 28 day experiment (Figure 10D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10C,D.

claim: After four days of infection, both VACV-WR and ΔA51R viruses replicated to similar titers in lung tissue.
source: After four days of infection, both VACV-WR and ΔA51R viruses replicated to similar titers in lung tissue, the primary site of infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from tissue virus titer measurements.

claim: By day 6, a trend toward lower ΔA51R titers in the lungs was observed, although this difference was not statistically significant.
source: By day 6, however, a trend toward lower ΔA51R titers in the lungs was observed, although this difference was not statistically significant (p=0.05; Figure 10E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10E.

claim: Neither VACV-WR nor ΔA51R viruses were detected in isolated ovaries by day 4 post-infection.
source: Neither VACV-WR nor ΔA51R viruses were detected in isolated ovaries by day 4 post-infection, suggesting that these viruses had not yet spread to this distant tissue.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from tissue virus titer measurements.

claim: By day 6 post-infection, significantly higher virus titers were detected in the ovaries of all VACV-WR-infected animals compared to ΔA51R-infected animals.
source: By day 6 post-infection, however, we detected significantly higher virus titers (p<0.05) in the ovaries of all VACV-WR-infected animals compared to ΔA51R-infected animals, in which virus was detectable in only 1/5 animals (Figure 10F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10F.

claim: A51R is important for VACV virulence in vivo.
source: These data suggest that A51R is not only important for VACV replication in cell culture but also for virulence in vivo.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the mouse infection studies showing reduced mortality and viral loads.

claim: The reduced replication of the ΔA51R strain at later time points was not caused by a reduction in the extracellular enveloped form of VACV.
source: The reduced replication of the ΔA51R strain at later time points of infection during in vitro and in vivo infections was not caused by a reduction in the extracellular enveloped (EEV) form of VACV, which primarily mediates spread of the virus (Smith et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from EEV measurements and citation for EEV function.

claim: Despite approximately 10-fold lower titers of total virus in ΔA51R cultures than in VACV-WR or ΔA51RFA51R cultures, ΔA51R cultures shed approximately twofold higher levels of EEV.
source: Our analysis revealed that, despite ∼10-fold lower titers of total (intracellular and extracellular) virus in ΔA51R cultures than in VACV-WR or ΔA51RFA51R cultures, ΔA51R cultures shed ∼twofold higher levels of EEV than VACV-WR or ΔA51RFA51R cultures (Figure 10—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1C.

claim: IFN pre-treatment reduced VACV-WR and ΔA51RFA51R titers by approximately 10-fold by 24 hpi relative to control treatment.
source: Comparing the titers of VACV-WR, ΔA51R, or ΔA51RFA51R cultures pre-treated with IFN to parallel cultures without IFN treatment, we found that IFN pre-treatment reduced VACV-WR and ΔA51RFA51R titers by ∼10-fold by 24 hpi relative to control treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from IFN pre-treatment experiments.

claim: ΔA51R titers were similarly reduced by IFN pre-treatment, suggesting that loss of A51R does not make VACV more susceptible to the antiviral effects of IFN.
source: ΔA51R titers, however, were similarly reduced at this time point, suggesting that loss of A51R does not make VACV more susceptible to the antiviral effects of IFN (Figure 10—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the IFN pre-treatment experiments shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Invertebrate model organisms have proven useful in elucidating a wide range of host responses to infection.
source: Invertebrate model organisms have proven useful in elucidating a wide range of host responses to infection and because many of these responses are well conserved, studies in model organisms are often directly relevant to human health (Moser et al., 2010; Panda and Cherry, 2012; Moy et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established scientific knowledge.

claim: Studies of invertebrate antiviral RNA interference pathways have produced powerful tools for probing and manipulating gene function.
source: Notably, studies of invertebrate antiviral RNA interference (RNAi) pathways (Fire et al., 1998; Zhou and Rana, 2013) have produced powerful tools for probing and manipulating gene function, with potential utility for direct therapeutic intervention (Blake et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established scientific knowledge.

claim: Relatively small genomes, well-defined genetics, and efficient RNAi pathways make insect models attractive systems in which to study virus-host interplay.
source: Relatively small genomes, well-defined genetics, and efficient RNAi pathways make insect models attractive systems in which to study virus-host interplay (Moser et al., 2010; Cherry, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established scientific knowledge.

claim: Dipteran organisms, such as Drosophila melanogaster, have been the primary focus of virus-host studies in invertebrates.
source: Dipteran organisms, such as Drosophila melanogaster, have been the primary focus of virus-host studies in invertebrates and Drosophila RNAi screens have greatly enhanced our understanding of how eukaryotic host factors can promote or inhibit virus replication (Cherry, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established scientific knowledge.

claim: Virus-host studies in invertebrates have almost exclusively focused on RNA viruses.
source: These studies have almost exclusively focused on RNA viruses (Xu and Cherry, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established scientific knowledge.

claim: Most virus-host studies in the order Lepidoptera have focused on DNA viruses, particularly baculoviruses.
source: In contrast to Dipterans, most virus-host studies in the order Lepidoptera (moths and butterflies) have focused on DNA viruses, particularly baculoviruses (Ikeda et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established scientific knowledge.

claim: Studies of baculoviruses have provided key insights into highly conserved mechanisms by which Lepidopterans combat DNA virus infection.
source: These studies have provided key insights into highly conserved mechanisms by which Lepidopterans combat DNA virus infection (Ikeda et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established scientific knowledge.

claim: Lepidopterans have not previously been used to probe restrictions to RNA virus replication.
source: Thus, while Lepidopterans provide a relevant model for studying DNA virus-host interaction they have not previously been used to probe restrictions to RNA virus replication.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the literature review showing focus on DNA viruses in Lepidoptera.

claim: The gypsy moth (Lymantria dispar) has been one of the most prolific North American hardwood forest pests since its accidental release in the late 1800's.
source: The gypsy moth (Lymantria dispar) has been one of the most prolific North American hardwood forest pests since its accidental release in the late 1800's (Sparks et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established knowledge.

claim: L. dispar-derived cell lines are susceptible to a wide variety of invertebrate DNA viruses.
source: L. dispar-derived cell lines are susceptible to a wide variety of invertebrate DNA viruses, and as such, they are often used in virus-host studies (Sparks and Gundersen-Rindal, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established knowledge.

claim: L. dispar-derived LD652 cells can support a limited infection by vaccinia virus.
source: Interestingly, L. dispar-derived LD652 cells can also support a limited infection by vaccinia virus (VACV), a vertebrate poxvirus encoding a large dsDNA genome (Li et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: During infection of LD652 cells, VACV undergoes early gene expression, DNA replication and late gene expression, but the infection is abortive due to a defect in one or more steps of virion morphogenesis.
source: During infection of LD652 cells, VACV undergoes early gene expression, DNA replication and late gene expression, but the infection is abortive due to a defect in one or more steps of virion morphogenesis (Li et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: VACV entry and early gene expression have been documented in Drosophila cells, however viral DNA replication and subsequent late gene expression were not detected.
source: VACV entry and early gene expression have also been documented in Drosophila cells, however viral DNA replication and subsequent late gene expression were not detected, indicating that VACV replication is blocked earlier in its life cycle in Drosophila cells than in LD652 cells (Moser et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: RNAi screening of VACV-infected Drosophila cells has identified multiple host factors required for VACV entry in eukaryotic hosts.
source: Despite these limitations, RNAi screening of VACV-infected Drosophila cells has identified multiple host factors required for VACV entry in eukaryotic hosts (Moser et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The LD652 cell culture system provides a unique model in which to explore multiple aspects of vertebrate DNA virus biology.
source: Thus, the LD652 cell culture system provides a unique model in which to explore multiple aspects of vertebrate DNA virus biology, including basic replication strategies and suppression of host immune pathways by viral proteins.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the characteristics of LD652 cells described in the literature.

claim: The extent of RNA virus studies in Lepidoptera is limited compared to DNA virus studies.
source: The extent of RNA virus studies in Lepidoptera is limited compared to DNA virus studies and largely restricted to non-enveloped dsRNA and (+)-sense ssRNA viruses such as cypoviruses (Hill et al., 1999), iflaviruses (van Oers, 2010) and tetraviruses (Short and Dorrington, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established knowledge.

claim: Several RNA viruses that infect Lepidoptera cannot productively replicate in cultured cells.
source: These viruses only infect invertebrate hosts and several cannot productively replicate in cultured cells (Short and Dorrington, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established knowledge.

claim: Negative-sense ssRNA viruses have not been previously reported to productively infect Lepidopteran hosts.
source: Furthermore, to our knowledge, (−)-sense ssRNA viruses have not been previously reported to productively infect Lepidopteran hosts.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: A new model system for studying RNA viruses in Lepidopteran hosts may be useful in the design of new biocontrol agents for pest species.
source: A new model system for studying RNA viruses in Lepidopteran hosts may be useful in the design of new biocontrol agents for pest species and improve our understanding of RNA virus-induced disease in vertebrates.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential applications.

claim: VSV and SINV replicate in a wide range of invertebrate and vertebrate hosts.
source: Here we explore RNA virus-Lepidopteran host interactions by infecting LD652 cells with the (−)-sense ssRNA vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) or the (+)-sense ssRNA Sindbis virus (SINV), both of which replicate in a wide range of invertebrate and vertebrate hosts (Letchworth et al., 1999; Xiong et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established knowledge.

claim: A51R may provide functions beyond microtubule stabilization that promote RNA virus replication.
source: These results suggest that MT stabilization alone is insufficient to promote full RNA virus rescue.
evidence: This claim is implicitly derived from the observation that the A51RR321A mutant stabilizes MTs but has reduced rescue activity.
